evidence_items.locator: Opening summary; methodology and Core Result
evidence_items.explanation: The February–June experiment found slowdown among 16 experienced developers completing 246 tasks in familiar open-source repositories. It supports that setting, and the authors explicitly reject generalizing it to most software development.

Agents successfully completed a measurable share of multi-step software and reasoning tasks, contradicting a categorical denial of task-level usefulness. A 50% success threshold also leaves substantial reliability limitations and does not establish dependable autonomous employment.

The analysis through November 2025 finds falling prices at fixed benchmark performance, opposing the comparable-output reading. It also reports that benchmark-running costs can remain flat or rise as models pursue higher performance, so it does not establish falling total spending or provider production costs.

evidence_items.locator: Opening results discussion, before Wider adoption
evidence_items.explanation: The follow-up begun in August 2025 produced point estimates favoring speedup, but confidence intervals included no effect and selection problems weakened inference. Its window is not isolated to the pre-publication period, so it limits extrapolation from the earlier study rather than deciding the December claim.

unresolved_gaps: The evidence does not establish an industry-wide average effect on developer productivity.
No common population or failure threshold defines the claim about all AI-powered products.
Public inference prices do not directly measure providers' production costs or total inference expenditure.
The exact state of all these capabilities on December 8 is not measured by a single contemporaneous study.
